d6e39f3d11.fzText: To be eligible for the final project, the midterm must be submitted on time; otherwise, the student may attend but will receive an FZ. The course includes unannounced in-class “pop-up” tasks completed only during class time; absence results in zero for that task (no make-ups).
weekly: Get to know each other. Why take this course? Introduction to Applied Sustainable Business Development. Course expectations, assessment methods, class participation and how to use course materials. Introduction to sustainability and sustainable development: key concepts, contemporary sustainability challenges, and their relevance to business and different professional fields. Hahn (2025), Chapters 1–2

The Business Case Market forces; public policy and regulation; the top line and competitive advantage; the Interface example; Exercise: Protecting Your Brand; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 3 as the main conceptual update, with selected material from Ch. 8 (government/regulation) and Ch. 10 (investors and sustainable finance).

Defining Sustainability Why are we doing this? Defining sustainability for your company; what sustainability means to employees and customers; translating sustainability into language different audiences can understand; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 2 for sustainability concepts, Triple Bottom Line, ESG and SDGs; selected Ch. 3 for business relevance

Understanding Your Stakeholders and What Is Material to Them Why stakeholder engagement matters; stakeholder mapping; materiality and the process for determining it; best practices and delivery mechanisms; communicating results back to stakeholders; the goal of multiple stakeholder touchpoints; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 6 as the main framework, supported by selected stakeholder perspectives from Ch. 7, 9, 10 and 11, plus Ch. 20 for materiality/reporting links.

Baselining Sustainability to Measure What Matters Measure what matters; inclusive and organizational boundaries; GHG reporting principles; KPIs; gap and SWOT analysis; sustainability data; hotspot identification; screening and full life-cycle assessment; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 18 (sustainability accounting, carbon accounting and life-cycle approaches) and Ch. 19 (management control, indicators and performance measurement).

Goals, Vision and Your Sustainability North Star The North Star; backcasting; incremental and magnitude-of-order goal-setting approaches; integrating corporate, departmental and individual goals; aligning KPIs with sustainability goals; assigning responsibility and accountability; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 19 for objectives, indicators, targets and sustainability management control; selected Ch. 4 for the scale and ambition of sustainability change.

Management Support Is Essential People need to see, hear and feel leadership support; budget; dedicated time and resources; governance support; proving the concept; small wins and momentum; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: selected Ch. 11–12 on top-management influence, employee-related sustainability and organizational structures; Ch. 19 where relevant to accountability and control.

Understanding Change Management to Guide Implementation Why change is difficult; change psychology; the Hagen-Wilhelm Change Matrix; understanding your company and your people; breaking down silos and coordinating across departments; engaging sceptics; sustaining momentum; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: selected Ch. 12 and Ch. 19 to connect change with sustainable HRM, organizational routines, management systems and control.
Midterm-project

Engaging Employees Around Sustainability Introduction to employee engagement; sustainability and employee engagement; training and making sustainability part of the job; making it personal; recognizing different learning styles; empowered employees; intrapreneurship; feedback, incentives and recognition; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 11–12 for sustainable employee behaviour, training, feedback, rewards, recognition, green teams and sustainable HRM.

Systems Decision Making and Internal Alignment Systems thinking for sustainability; interconnections, feedback loops, delays and leverage points; prioritizing actions; incorporating sustainability into decision-making and systems; investment and procurement policies; supply-chain and operational alignment; 8 Wastes of Lean as a resource-efficiency lens; operationalizing green teams; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 14–15 for sustainable supply chains, production and logistics; selected Ch. 19 for management systems and internal alignment.

Institutionalizing Sustainability Job descriptions and onboarding; evaluation and alignment of benefits; reward, recognition and compensation; gamification; accountability; embedding sustainability into organizational routines and processes; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 12 and Ch. 19 for sustainable HRM, structural measures, accountability, performance management and control.

Communicating Sustainability Internal communication; continuous communication to reinforce the message; sharing both good and bad performance; aligning communication efforts; internal social media; external reporting; transparency and trust; credible sustainability claims; Lessons Learned. Hahn integration: Ch. 16 (sustainability marketing and communication) and Ch. 20 (sustainability reporting, materiality and reporting frameworks).
Interdisciplinary final project; project presentations; poster presentations; integration of the Wilhelm implementation framework with the updated Hahn concepts and tools.

weekly: Introduction to the course, course expectations, and AI policy. Diversity, equality, equity, inclusion, and belonging. The business case for diversity. Introduction to equality as a legal obligation in Türkiye, including selected provisions of the Turkish Constitution, Labour Law No. 4857, and Law No. 6701. Türkiye opening case on gendered occupations: nursing and cabin crew. Harvey Section 1; Triana Chapter 1.

Social categorization and social identity. Differences between stereotypes, prejudice, discrimination, and bias. Privilege and its effects on life experiences. Examining one’s own perspectives on difference. Differences, group dynamics, and conflict. Harvey Section 1; Triana Chapter 2 and selected material from Chapter 14.

Organizational diversity and inclusion. Diversity as a potential source of creativity, information, problem solving, and performance. Challenges associated with diverse teams. Organizational conditions required for inclusion and effective diversity management. International and national organizational examples and in-class activities. Harvey Section 1; Triana Chapters 1 and 13.

Race and ethnicity as social and organizational categories. Primary and secondary dimensions of diversity. Multiple group memberships, saliency, cultural identity, stereotyping, and discrimination. Türkiye and international organizational contexts. Harvey Section 2; Triana Chapter 4

National origin, immigration and migration, language and accent, multicultural workplaces, intercultural communication, and cultural intelligence. Organizational adaptation to increasingly diverse workforces. Midterm Project introduction and instructions. Harvey Section 2; Triana Chapter 10.

Gender inequality, occupational segregation, women and leadership, gender stereotypes, masculinity, sexual orientation, workplace inclusion, harassment, and organizational responses. Harvey Section 3; Triana Chapters 5 and 6.

Age diversity and ageism in organizations. Disability, barriers to employment, reasonable accommodation, accessibility, universal design, and neurodiversity. Inclusive workplace practices. Harvey Section 3; Triana Chapters 8 and 9.

Social class, religion and belief, appearance and weight, family responsibilities, pregnancy, caregiving, and work–life issues. Multiple social identities, saliency, and intersectionality. Midterm Project presentations begin. Harvey Section 4; Triana Chapters 7, 11 and 12.

Completion of individual midterm presentations. Integration of concepts covered during the first half of the course. Introduction to the interdisciplinary Final Project, team formation, project expectations, and preliminary topic discussion.

Employment discrimination and equality legislation in Türkiye and selected international contexts. Genuine occupational requirements and justified differentiation. Ethical implications of diversity management, media representation, diverse consumers, and inclusive marketing. Harvey Section 5; Triana Chapter 3 and selected related chapters.

Team diversity and organizational dynamics. Implicit bias in recruitment, promotion, evaluation, and decision-making. Inclusive leadership, mentoring, employee resource groups, diversity training, flexible work practices, accountability, and emerging organizational issues. Harvey Section 5; Triana Chapters 13, 14 and 15.

Belonging and psychological inclusion. Recognizing and managing workplace bullying. Organizational accountability and contemporary EDI challenges. Integration of course concepts through real-world cases requiring the application of theory, law, ethics, evidence, and managerial reasoning. Harvey Sections 5 and 6; selected Triana Opening and Closing Cases

Diversity audit and organizational diagnosis. Synthesizing course theories, cases, exercises, and evidence. Developing practical and evidence-based recommendations for improving equality, diversity, inclusion, and belonging. Preparation for the Final Project Defense. Harvey Section 7; Triana Chapters 12, 13 and 15.
Team poster presentations and project defense. Approximately 15 minutes per team, followed by questions, peer evaluation, discussion, and overall course integration
